topic.title: Reverse percentages: finding the original quantity
topic.subject: maths
topic.examWeightHint: M3 and M4 are the calculator papers (2 hours, 100 marks) and this is a fixture on both: one straight reversal of 3 marks, late on M3 (Summer 2024 Q27, November 2025 Q30, Summer 2026 Q26) and early to middle on M4 (Summer 2023 Q7, Summer 2024 Q11, November 2025 Q15, Summer 2026 Q2), and in most series a second item of 4 marks where the reversal is followed by another step or by a second reversal (Summer 2025 M3 Q22 and M4 Q19, November 2024 M3 Q24 and M4 Q10). The scheme prints three combined method-and-accuracy lines — '(100 ± r)% = the value', '1% = ...', '100% = ...' — and credits the single division by the multiplier as an alternative worth the same three marks; a fourth mark is added for the step to the quantity actually requested and follows through from your own original. On M7 and M8 Paper 1 the same skill appears without a calculator at 2-4 marks in the first half of the paper (Summer 2024 M7 Q1, Summer 2025 M7 Q3, Summer 2026 M7 Q2 and Q8), with numbers chosen so that 10% or 5% is the sensible unit rather than 1%.
mustMemorise: Multiplier: increase of r% is × (1 + r/100), decrease of r% is × (1 − r/100)
Original = final ÷ multiplier — ÷ 1.28 after a 28% increase, ÷ 0.818 after an 18.2% decrease
Unitary route the schemes print: (100 ± r)% = the value, ÷ (100 ± r) for 1%, × 100 for the original
Two changes need two divisions, taken in reverse order; yearly rates are never added
Money answers to two decimal places
notOnThisSpec: The compound-interest formula with an index, P(1 + r)ⁿ, and any question asking for the number of years or the rate: those belong to the M8 growth-and-decay statement M8-NA-04, not to M3-NA-02.
More than three repeated changes: the Teacher Guidance on M2-NA-08 restricts compound interest to three iterations, so a reversal never has more than three multipliers to undo.
Percentage error, and continuous or exponential growth to base e: neither appears in the CCEA statements.
Reverse percentages applied to upper and lower bounds — bounds are M3-NA-03 and are examined on their own.

note.title: Reverse percentages: finding the original quantity
note.subject: maths

mustKnow: Multiplier for an increase of r%: 1 + r/100. For a decrease: 1 − r/100.
Original = final ÷ multiplier (÷ 1.28 after a 28% increase, ÷ 0.818 after an 18.2% decrease).
Unitary route: (100 ± r)% = the value, then ÷ (100 ± r) for 1%, then × 100.
Two changes: two multipliers forwards, two divisions backwards; rates are never added.
Money answers carry two decimal places.

notOnThisSpec: The compound-interest formula with an index, P(1 + r)ⁿ, and any question asking for the number of years or the rate: those belong to the M8 growth-and-decay statement M8-NA-04, not to M3-NA-02.
More than three repeated changes: the Teacher Guidance on M2-NA-08 restricts compound interest to three iterations, so a reversal never has more than three multipliers to undo.
Percentage error, and continuous or exponential growth to base e: neither appears in the CCEA statements.
Reverse percentages applied to upper and lower bounds — bounds are M3-NA-03 and are examined on their own.

mustBeAbleTo: Write the multiplier for any percentage change: an increase of 8% is × 1.08, a decrease of 15% is × 0.85, an increase of 2.5% is × 1.025.
Decide, before calculating, whether the number in the question sits before or after the change, and write the line '(100 ± r)% = that number'.
Reverse the change by dividing by the multiplier, or by finding 1% and multiplying by 100 — never by taking the percentage of the value you were given.
Recognise the after value inside the wording: a sale price, a price including VAT at 20%, a population after growth, a value after depreciation, a price that is r% more than another.
Handle a difference: when you are told the difference between two amounts and one is r% more than the other, the difference is the r%, not the 100%.
Reverse two changes in a row, undoing the most recent one first, and check by running the chain forwards.
Take the last step to the quantity the question asks for: the saving, the profit, the difference or the later price.
Work out a change as a percentage of the original — change ÷ original × 100 — and see that this is the same relationship read forwards.
Apply and reverse two different rates in successive years, giving money to two decimal places.
Do all of this without a calculator on Paper 1 by choosing 10%, 5% or a fraction as the unit instead of 1%.
sheet.howExamined: M3 and M4 are the calculator papers (2 hours, 100 marks) and this is a fixture on both: one straight reversal of 3 marks, late on M3 (Summer 2024 Q27, November 2025 Q30, Summer 2026 Q26) and early to middle on M4 (Summer 2023 Q7, Summer 2024 Q11, November 2025 Q15, Summer 2026 Q2), and in most series a second item of 4 marks where the reversal is followed by another step or by a second reversal (Summer 2025 M3 Q22 and M4 Q19, November 2024 M3 Q24 and M4 Q10). The scheme prints three combined method-and-accuracy lines — '(100 ± r)% = the value', '1% = ...', '100% = ...' — and credits the single division by the multiplier as an alternative worth the same three marks; a fourth mark is added for the step to the quantity actually requested and follows through from your own original. On M7 and M8 Paper 1 the same skill appears without a calculator at 2-4 marks in the first half of the paper (Summer 2024 M7 Q1, Summer 2025 M7 Q3, Summer 2026 M7 Q2 and Q8), with numbers chosen so that 10% or 5% is the sensible unit rather than 1%.
traps: Taking r% of the value you were given and adding or subtracting it — the majority approach on Summer 2024 M3 Q27 and M4 Q11, and worth nothing, because that percentage was worked out on the smaller original.
Equating the value to (100 − r)% after an increase, or to (100 + r)% after a decrease — Summer 2024 M4 Q11 saw 72% used for a 28% increase.
Reading 'depreciated' as a rise: November 2025 M3 Q30 and M4 Q15 saw 106.2% used where the value was 93.8% of the original.
Undoing × 1.2 by multiplying by 0.8 — those two do not cancel (1.2 × 0.8 = 0.96), only ÷ 1.2 does.
Reversing only one of two changes, or adding one rate back and taking the other off: about 37% reached full marks on November 2024 M4 Q10.

Stopping at the original when the question wanted the saving, the difference or the later price — the loss reported on Summer 2025 M3 Q22, and the wrong subtraction after the second percentage on M4 Q19.
Stopping at 1%: Summer 2023 M3 Q18 turned on the single line '81.8% = the value', and the candidates who wrote it almost always finished, but the last line has to say 100%.
Dividing the wrong pair for a percentage change: Summer 2025 M1 Q23 and M2 Q15 produced 108% and 92% far more often than the correct 8%, from new ÷ original or change ÷ new.
Applying two different yearly rates by adding them: Summer 2024 M3 Q19 found year two worked on the original deposit or the two rates summed.
Leaving money as 4820.5 rather than £4820.50: Summer 2023 M4 Q1 lost a mark to exactly that, and every money answer here needs two decimal places.

Opening with r% of the amount in front of you and then adding or subtracting it, which earns nothing: the first line has to equate that amount to (100 − r)% and work up to 100%, and it was that opening line candidates missed on Summer 2023 M4 Q7.

Adding the percentage back on instead of dividing it out, then carrying that figure into the second reversal: the first two marks came from equating the amount given to 90% and undoing the later change first, and very few candidates reached them on November 2024 M3 Q24.

workedExamples.stem: The annual membership fee at a leisure centre was increased by 24%. The new fee is £930. Work out the fee before the increase.

figure.alt: Two bars. The upper bar is ten blocks long, labelled 100% = £750. The lower bar is longer, labelled 124% = £930, with a dashed line marking where 100% ends. A downward arrow between them reads times 1.24 and an upward arrow reads divided by 1.24.

steps.decision: Before anything else I decide which side of the change the given number sits on. The fee was increased and then I was told the new fee, so £930 is the larger amount. That single decision is what separates the three-mark answers from the nothing answers.

options: £930 is the amount after the increase, so it is more than 100% of the old fee
£930 is the amount before the increase, so it is 100%
£930 is the increase itself, so it is 24%
whyMenu.explain: The question gives the new fee and asks for the old one. The new fee is the old fee plus 24% of it, so it is 124% of the old fee.

steps.decision: The multiplier for an increase of r% is 1 + r/100; for a decrease it is 1 − r/100. Writing the line '124% = £930' is the first mark on every CCEA scheme for this question type.

Divide by 124 to get down to 1%. On a calculator paper the alternative single line £930 ÷ 1.24 earns the same credit, but the unitary route is the one the scheme prints and it leaves a mark-bearing trail.
Multiply the 1% back up to 100%. Stopping at £7.50 is a real loss of the last mark; the answer line wants 100%, not 1%.

options: Multiply the 1% value by 100 to reach the original fee
whyMenu.explain: Subtracting 24% of £930 takes 24% of the wrong amount, and multiplying by 1.24 goes forwards again. Only ÷ 1.24 (or 1% then × 100) undoes the increase.

steps.decision: Ten seconds of checking. Multiply the answer forward by the same multiplier; if it does not land on the number in the question, the direction was the other way round.

twin.stem: A season ticket rose in price by 35%. It now costs £1026. Work out the price before the rise.

workedExamples.stem: In a clearance sale every pair of walking boots is reduced by 15%. A pair now costs £73.95. How much is saved by buying the boots in the sale?

steps.working: Sale price = after the reduction, so $85\% = £73.95$
steps.decision: A sale price is always the after value. A reduction of 15% leaves 85%, so the given price is 85% of the ticket price and the answer must be larger than £73.95.
Divide by 85, not by 15. The 15 is the size of the reduction; the 85 is what the price you were given represents.
That is the price before the sale. On the single-line route it is £73.95 ÷ 0.85 = £87, which the scheme credits just the same.

Read the question again. It asks how much is saved, not what the boots used to cost, so one subtraction still stands between £87 and the mark. Summer 2025 examiners reported exactly this step being left out.

options: The saving is the original price minus the sale price
The saving is 15% of the sale price
The saving is the original price, because that is what was found
whyMenu.explain: 15% of £73.95 is £11.09, which is 15% of the wrong amount. The saving is 15% of the original: £87 − £73.95 = £13.05, and 0.15 × £87 = £13.05 agrees.

steps.decision: Two checks in one line: the saving is 15% of the original, and the original times 0.85 returns the sale price.

twin.stem: A coat is reduced by 12% in a sale and now costs £171.60. How much is saved by buying it in the sale?

workedExamples.stem: In 2025 a flat was sold for £184 320, a loss of 4% on what the seller had paid for it. She had bought the flat in 2021 from an owner who made a profit of 20% on that sale. Work out how much the 2021 owner had originally paid for the flat.

steps.working: Two changes → two reversals, taken in reverse order.
steps.decision: The flat changed hands twice, so the chain runs: 2021 owner's price → +20% → the 2025 seller's price → −4% → £184 320. Working backwards means undoing the last change first.
A loss is a decrease, so the 2025 sale price is 96% of what the seller paid. Writing this line is the mark; the November 2024 report found that few candidates even reached it.
Divide by the multiplier 0.96. The unitary version is £184 320 ÷ 96 = £1920 for 1%, then × 100.
Now reverse the first change. The £192 000 she paid is 120% of what the earlier owner paid, because he added 20% on top of his own price.

options: £192 000 is 120% of the earlier owner's price
£192 000 is 80% of the earlier owner's price
£192 000 is 100% and 20% of it is the profit
whyMenu.explain: He sold for more than he paid, so his selling price is above 100%. Taking 20% of £192 000 would take 20% of the wrong amount.

steps.decision: Second reversal done. Two changes, two divisions: ÷ 0.96 then ÷ 1.2, never one division and one subtraction.
Running the chain forwards lands back on the number in the question, so both directions were taken the right way round.

twin.stem: A van was sold for £27 300, a loss of 9% on what its owner had paid. He had bought it from a dealer who made a profit of 25% on that sale. How much had the dealer paid for the van?

workedExamples.stem:
Paper 1, no calculator.
(a) The population of a village rose from 2500 to 2900. Work out the percentage increase.
(b) The population of a second village also rose to 2900, and that was an increase of 16%. Work out the second village's population before the rise.

steps.decision: A percentage change always starts with the change itself. Without the 400 on the page there is nothing for the first mark to be given for.

The denominator is the original, the figure the change started from. Dividing 2900 by 2500 gives 116%, which is the multiplier as a percentage, not the increase; dividing 400 by 2900 uses the new figure and gives 13.8%.

options: 400 ÷ 2500 × 100, because the increase is measured against the population it started from
2900 ÷ 2500 × 100, because that compares the two populations
400 ÷ 2900 × 100, because 2900 is the population being described
whyMenu.explain: 2900 ÷ 2500 = 116%, which is the whole new population as a percentage of the old, not the rise. The rise is the 16 percentage points above 100.

steps.working: (b) The rise has already happened, so $116\% = 2900$
steps.decision: Same two numbers, opposite direction. Here 2900 is the after value, so it is 116% of the population before the rise, and the answer must come out below 2900.

whyMenu.explain: The population went up, so the figure you are given is above 100%. 84% would be a decrease of 16%.

steps.decision: No calculator, so keep the arithmetic friendly: 116 × 25 = 2900, so 1% is 25. Short division by 116 is quicker than long division by 1.16.
Multiply back up to 100%. On Paper 1 the unitary route is almost always the quicker one, because ÷ 1.16 by hand is unpleasant and ÷ 116 is not.

steps.working: Notice: part (a) and part (b) are one change read in two directions — $2500 \times 1.16 = 2900$.
steps.decision: Forward you multiply by 1.16; backward you divide by 1.16. Every question in this topic is one of those two sentences in disguise.

twin.stem: A shop's monthly sales fell by 7.5% to £7400. Work out the sales before the fall.

items.stem: Which multiplier increases an amount by 8%?
items.skill: Write the multiplier for a percentage increase

options.feedback: An increase of r% is a multiplier of 1 + r/100, so 8% gives 1.08. The 1 keeps what you started with; the 0.08 adds the extra.
0.08 is the increase on its own, so multiplying by it leaves only the extra 8% and throws away the original amount. Add the 1.
0.92 is the multiplier for a decrease of 8%. Increases sit above 1, decreases below it.

items.stem: Which multiplier decreases an amount by 15%?
items.skill: Write the multiplier for a percentage decrease

options.feedback: A decrease of 15% leaves 85% of the amount, so the multiplier is 0.85.
1.15 increases by 15%. Check the direction word before you write the multiplier.
0.15 gives the size of the reduction, not the reduced amount. What is left is 100% − 15% = 85%.

items.stem: A price was increased by 12%. The new price is £56. Which first line earns the method mark?
items.skill: Set up the first line of a reverse percentage

options.feedback: The price you are given comes after the increase, so it is 100% + 12% of the old price. Every CCEA scheme for this question type gives its first mark for this line.
That takes 12% of the new price. The 12% was worked out on the old price, which is smaller, so this figure is too big and the line earns nothing.
88% would be right after a decrease of 12%. An increase puts the given value above 100%.

items.stem: An amount was multiplied by 1.2. Which single operation gets back to the amount you started with?

options.feedback: Multiplying and dividing by the same number undo each other. This is the whole of reverse percentages in one line.
0.8 and 1.2 do not undo each other: 1.2 × 0.8 = 0.96, so you land 4% below where you began. Only ÷ 1.2 returns the original.
Subtracting 20% is the same as multiplying by 0.8, and 20% of the larger amount is bigger than the 20% that was added on.

items.stem: A van has depreciated in value by 6%. It is now worth £11 750. The £11 750 is
items.skill: Read a direction word (depreciation) and place the given value

options.text: 94% of its value before the depreciation
options.feedback: Depreciation is a fall in value, so 6% has gone and 94% is left. £11 750 ÷ 0.94 = £12 500.

options.text: 106% of its value before the depreciation
options.feedback: 106% would mean the van had gained value. Depreciation always puts the given value below 100%.

options.text: 6% of its value before the depreciation
options.feedback: 6% is the size of the fall, not what is left. The van still holds most of its value.

items.stem: A shop bought a bicycle for £250 and sold it for £285. Which calculation gives the percentage profit?
items.skill: Choose the base for a percentage change

options.feedback: Change divided by the original, times 100. The profit is £35 and it is measured against the £250 the shop paid, giving 14%.
That gives 114%, the selling price as a percentage of the cost price. The profit is the 14 percentage points above 100, and this line on its own earns nothing.
The change is divided by the new value here, giving 12.3%. A percentage change is always measured against the amount it started from.

items.stem: £4000 is invested. It earns 3% in the first year and 1.5% in the second year. Which calculation gives the value after two years?
items.skill: Apply two different rates in successive years

options.feedback: Each year acts on the balance at the start of that year, so the multipliers follow one another: £4181.80.
The two rates have been added. 1.03 × 1.015 = 1.04545, not 1.045, so this comes out at £4180, which is £1.80 short, and the accuracy mark goes.
Both years have been worked on the original £4000 and then added together, which more than doubles the money. Year two acts on the year-one balance.

items.stem: A coat's sale price is £68 after a reduction of 15%. The question asks how much is saved. What goes on the answer line?
items.skill: Take the last step to the quantity the question asks for

options.feedback: £68 ÷ 0.85 = £80 before the sale, and the saving is £80 − £68 = £12. The reverse step is the middle of the question, not the end.
£80 is the price before the sale, which is correct working but not what was asked. One subtraction stands between it and the mark.
That is 15% of the sale price. The 15% was taken off the original £80, so the saving is 15% of £80, not of £68.

parts.stem: Write down the multiplier that increases an amount by 8%.
hints: An increase keeps the whole amount and adds more, so the multiplier is above 1.
100% + 8% = 108%, and 108% as a decimal is

0.92 is the multiplier for a decrease of 8%. Read the direction word, then decide whether the multiplier sits above or below 1.

context.setting: No context: the multiplier on its own

parts.stem: Write down the multiplier that decreases an amount by 15%.
hints: A decrease leaves part of the amount behind, so the multiplier is below 1.
100% − 15% = 85%, and 85% as a decimal is

commonErrors.feedback: 0.15 is the change on its own. Multiplying by it gives only the 15%, not the amount that results. The multiplier takes the change from the whole: 0.85.
1.15 is the multiplier for an increase of 15%. Read the direction word, then decide whether the multiplier sits above or below 1.

context.setting: A guitar in a music shop

parts.stem:
The price of a guitar was increased by 18%. The new price is £1475.
Work out the price of the guitar before the increase.

scheme.examinerNote: The single-division route £1475 ÷ 1.18 = £1250 is credited mark for mark as the alternative solution (M1 A1 A1), as CCEA schemes print it.

accept: £1250 on the answer line, with or without a trailing .00

hints: Decide first: is £1475 the amount before the change or after it?
118% = £1475. Divide by 118 to reach 1%.

commonErrors.feedback: That is 18% of £1475 taken off. The 18% was worked out on the original amount, which is smaller, so it comes to a different figure. Start with 118% = £1475.
The division was done with 0.82, the multiplier for a change the other way. An increase means the value you are given is above 100%.
£12.50 is 1%, which earns the second mark. The answer line wants 100%, so multiply it by 100 before you write it down.

context.setting: A second-hand motorbike

parts.stem:
The price of a motorbike was reduced by 12%. It now costs £3740.
Work out the price of the motorbike before the reduction.

scheme.examinerNote: The single-division route £3740 ÷ 0.88 = £4250 is credited mark for mark as the alternative solution (M1 A1 A1), as CCEA schemes print it.

accept: £4250 on the answer line, with or without a trailing .00

hints: Decide first: is £3740 the amount before the change or after it?
88% = £3740. Divide by 88 to reach 1%.

commonErrors.feedback: That is 12% of £3740 added on. The 12% was worked out on the original amount, which is larger, so it comes to a different figure. Start with 88% = £3740.
The division was done with 1.12, the multiplier for a change the other way. A decrease, and depreciation is a decrease, means the value you are given is below 100%.

context.setting: A delivery van that has lost value

parts.stem:
A delivery van has depreciated in value by 6.5%. It is now worth £29 172.
What was the van worth before the depreciation?

scheme.examinerNote: The single-division route £29 172 ÷ 0.935 = £31 200 is credited mark for mark as the alternative solution (M1 A1 A1), as CCEA schemes print it.

accept: £31 200 on the answer line, with or without a trailing .00

hints: Decide first: is £29 172 the amount before the change or after it?
93.5% = £29 172. Divide by 93.5 to reach 1%.

commonErrors.feedback: That is 6.5% of £29 172 added on. The 6.5% was worked out on the original amount, which is larger, so it comes to a different figure. Start with 93.5% = £29 172.
The division was done with 1.065, the multiplier for a change the other way. A decrease, and depreciation is a decrease, means the value you are given is below 100%.
Multiplying by 0.935 applies the depreciation for a second time instead of undoing it. To undo × 0.935 you divide by 0.935.

context.setting: A laptop invoice that includes VAT

parts.stem:
A laptop costs £514.80 including VAT at 20%.
Work out the cost of the laptop before VAT was added.

scheme.examinerNote: The single-division route £514.80 ÷ 1.2 = £429 is credited mark for mark as the alternative solution (M1 A1 A1), as CCEA schemes print it.

accept: £429 on the answer line, with or without a trailing .00

hints: Decide first: is £514.80 the amount before the change or after it?
120% = £514.80. Divide by 120 to reach 1%.

commonErrors.feedback: That is 20% of £514.80 taken off. The 20% was worked out on the original amount, which is smaller, so it comes to a different figure. Start with 120% = £514.80.
The division was done with 0.8, the multiplier for a change the other way. An increase means the value you are given is above 100%.
Multiplying by 0.8 is not the opposite of multiplying by 1.2: 1.2 × 0.8 = 0.96, so this lands 4% low. Divide by 1.2.

context.setting: The population of a town after new housing

parts.stem:
The population of a town increased by 12.5% over ten years. The population is now 33 750.
Calculate the population ten years ago.

scheme.examinerNote: The single-division route 33 750 ÷ 1.125 = 30 000 is credited mark for mark as the alternative solution (M1 A1 A1), as CCEA schemes print it.

hints: Decide first: is 33 750 the amount before the change or after it?
112.5% = 33 750. Divide by 112.5 to reach 1%.

commonErrors.feedback: That is 12.5% of 33 750 taken off. The 12.5% was worked out on the original amount, which is smaller, so it comes to a different figure. Start with 112.5% = 33 750.
The division was done with 0.875, the multiplier for a change the other way. An increase means the value you are given is above 100%.

context.setting: A theatre ticket on the non-calculator paper

parts.stem:
Paper 1: no calculator.
The price of a theatre ticket rose by 20% to £54.
Work out the price of the ticket before the rise.
hints: The £54 comes after the rise, so it is 120% of the old price.
Without a calculator, go through 10% rather than 1%: 120% = £54, so 10% = £4.50.

commonErrors.feedback: That is £54 less 20% of £54. The 20% was added to £45, so it was £9, not £10.80. Divide by 1.2 instead.

context.setting: A jacket in a shop window on the non-calculator paper

parts.stem:
Paper 1: no calculator.
A jacket is reduced by 25% in a sale. The sale price is £54.
Work out the price of the jacket before the sale.
hints: A reduction of 25% leaves three quarters, so £54 is 75% of the old price.
Three quarters is £54, so one quarter is £18.
Four quarters: £18 × 4 = £72.

commonErrors.feedback: That is £54 with 25% of £54 added on. The £54 is only 75% of the original, so 25% of it is not the reduction. Three quarters is £54, so one quarter is £18.
Multiplying by 0.75 applies the reduction a second time. To undo a reduction you divide by 0.75.

context.setting: A pair of trainers in a clearance sale

parts.stem:
A pair of trainers is reduced by 35% in a clearance sale. The sale price is £84.50.
Calculate how much is saved by buying the trainers in the sale.

scheme.examinerNote: Follow through from the candidate's own original price.

hints: The sale price is after the reduction, so it is 65% of the ticket price.
£84.50 ÷ 0.65 gives the ticket price.
Read the question again: it asks for the saving, so subtract the sale price from the ticket price.

commonErrors.feedback: Three marks for reaching the ticket price. The question asks for the saving, so one subtraction is still owed: £130 − £84.50.
That is 35% of the sale price. The 35% was taken off the ticket price of £130, so the saving is 0.35 × £130 = £45.50.

context.setting: Two sizes of paint tub in a hardware shop

parts.stem:
A large tub of paint costs 35% more than a small tub.
The difference between the two prices is £9.45.
Work out the cost of the large tub.

scheme.for: 35% = £9.45 (the difference is the 35%, not the price)

hints: Draw the two tubs as bars. The small tub is 100%; the large tub is 135%. Which part of the picture is £9.45?
The overhang is the difference, and it is 35% of the small tub's price.
£9.45 ÷ 35 × 100 gives the small tub. The question asks for the large one.
parts.workedSolution: The difference is the extra 35%, so $35\% = £9.45$ and $1\% = £0.27$. Small tub $= £27$; large tub $= £27 + £9.45 = £36.45$, and $£27 \times 1.35 = £36.45$ agrees.

commonErrors.feedback: Three marks for the small tub. The question asks for the large tub, so add the difference back: £27 + £9.45.
£9.45 ÷ 1.35 = £7 treats the difference as the whole large price. The £9.45 is only the extra 35%, so divide by 35 and multiply by 100.

context.setting: A holiday caravan sold twice

parts.stem:
A holiday caravan was sold in 2025 for £47 610, a loss of 8% on what its owner had paid for it.
The owner had bought the caravan from a dealer who made a profit of 15% on that sale.
Work out how much the dealer had paid for the caravan.
hints: Two changes happened, so two reversals are needed, starting with the most recent.
A loss of 8% makes the 2025 price 92% of what the owner paid: £47 610 ÷ 0.92.
Now undo the dealer's 15% profit: £51 750 ÷ 1.15.
parts.workedSolution: $92\% = £47\,610$ so the owner paid $£51\,750$. Then $115\% = £51\,750$ so the dealer paid $£45\,000$. Forward check: $45\,000 \times 1.15 \times 0.92 = 47\,610$.

commonErrors.feedback: Both changes were undone by adding and subtracting percentages of the figures given. Each reversal is a division: ÷ 0.92 and then ÷ 1.15.
Two marks for the first reversal. That is what the owner paid; the question asks what the dealer paid, so the 15% profit still has to be reversed.

context.setting: A savings account with two different rates

parts.stem:
£6500 is put into a savings account.
The account pays 2.5% in the first year and 1.2% in the second year.
Calculate the value of the account after two years.

scheme.examinerNote: The second rate must act on the year-one balance, not on £6500.

hints: Two rates, two multipliers, applied one after the other.
Year 1: £6500 × 1.025. Write that balance down before you start year 2.
Year 2 acts on the new balance: × 1.012. Money answers carry two decimal places.

commonErrors.feedback: The rates were added to make 3.7%. 1.025 × 1.012 = 1.0373, so this is £1.95 short. Apply the multipliers one after the other.
The second year's 1.2% was taken on the original £6500 instead of on the year-one balance of £6662.50, which is simple interest, not compound.
The arithmetic is right but the money is not: £6742.45 has two decimal places and £6742.5 loses the accuracy mark.

context.setting: A savings account whose opening balance is unknown

parts.stem:
An account pays 4% in the first year and 1.5% in the second year.
After two years the account holds £5489.12.
Work out how much was put into the account at the start.
hints: Two years of growth, so two divisions, undoing the most recent year first.

commonErrors.feedback: The rates were added to make 5.5%. The combined multiplier is 1.04 × 1.015 = 1.0556, not 1.055, so this route lands on £5202.96 instead of £5200.
Taking 4% and then 1.5% off the final balance takes the percentages of the wrong amounts. Each year is undone by dividing.

context.setting: Membership of a swimming club on the non-calculator paper

parts.stem:
Paper 1: no calculator.
Membership of a swimming club rose by 84 members to 684.
Calculate the percentage increase in membership.

scheme.examinerNote: The division must be by the original membership, not by 684.

hints: The rise has already been given, so you do not have to work it out; what you do not have yet is the membership it started from.
684 − 84 = 600 members before the rise.
Percentage increase = increase ÷ original × 100 = 84 ÷ 600 × 100.

commonErrors.feedback: 684 ÷ 600 × 100 = 114%, the new membership as a percentage of the old. The increase is the 14 percentage points above 100, and without that step the line scores nothing.
The increase was divided by 684. A percentage change is measured against the amount it started from, so the denominator is 600.

context.setting: A printing machine sold on after three years

parts.stem:
A printing machine was bought for £18 500 and sold three years later for £12 025.
Calculate the percentage loss.
hints: Find the loss in pounds first; it is what the mark scheme looks for before anything else.
Percentage loss = loss ÷ cost price × 100.

commonErrors.feedback: 12 025 ÷ 18 500 × 100 = 65%, which is what the machine is still worth as a percentage of its cost. The loss is the remaining 35 percentage points.
The loss was divided by the selling price. Percentage profit and percentage loss are both measured against the cost price.

context.setting: The annual fee at a climbing centre

parts.stem:
The annual fee at a climbing centre was increased by 16%.
The new fee is £324.80.
What was the fee before the increase?

scheme.examinerNote: The single-division route £324.80 ÷ 1.16 = £280 is credited mark for mark as the alternative solution (M1 A1 A1), as CCEA schemes print it.

accept: £280 on the answer line, with or without a trailing .00

hints: The fee you are given is the one after the increase.

commonErrors.feedback: 16% of £324.80 was taken off. That 16% was worked out on the old fee of £280, so it was £44.80, not £51.97. The first line has to be 116% = £324.80.
The fee was equated to 84% instead of 116%. An increase leaves the given value above 100%, so divide by 1.16.
£2.80 is 1%, which earns two of the three marks. Multiply by 100 to reach the fee itself.

context.setting: A racing bicycle resold twice, with a trade price nobody is told

figures.alt: Three boxes: trade price (unknown), the shop's sale to Aoife at £2296, and the price Aoife later sold for (unknown). An arrow from the trade price to Aoife's purchase price reads times 1.12, with a dashed arrow back reading divided by 1.12. A longer arrow from the trade price round to Aoife's selling price reads times 1.225.

parts.stem:
A wholesaler supplies racing bicycles to shops at a trade price.
A shop sold one of the bicycles to Aoife for £2296 and so made a profit of 12% on the trade price.
Aoife later sold the same bicycle for 22.5% more than the trade price.
Calculate the profit that Aoife made.

scheme.examinerNote: Method only: the division has to be set up against 112%, and an accuracy mark cannot follow a method mark that was not earned.
The subtraction is from the £2296 Aoife paid, not from the trade price.

hints: The shop's 12% profit was made on the trade price, so the £2296 is 112% of the trade price.
£2296 ÷ 1.12 gives the trade price, and the 22.5% is then taken on that same trade price.
Aoife paid £2296 and sold for £2511.25, so her profit is the difference between those two.
parts.workedSolution: $112\% = £2296$, so the trade price is $£2050$. Aoife sold for $2050 \times 1.225 = £2511.25$ and had paid $£2296$, so her profit is $£2511.25 - £2296 = £215.25$.

commonErrors.feedback: Finding 12% of £2296 takes the percentage of the selling price rather than the trade price it was worked out on, and it answers a question that was not asked. Start with 112% = £2296.
Three marks for reaching Aoife's selling price. The question asks for her profit, so subtract what she paid: £2511.25 − £2296.
£461.25 is the rise on the trade price, which is the wholesaler's view of it. Aoife's profit is measured against the £2296 that she paid.

context.setting: A winter coat in a closing-down sale

parts.stem:
Paper 1: no calculator.
Write down the multiplier that decreases an amount by 45%.

accept: 55% or 55/100 written instead of the decimal

hints: A decrease of 45% leaves 100% − 45%.
55% as a decimal.

commonErrors.feedback: 0.45 is the part taken away. The multiplier is what is left: 0.55.

parts.stem:
A coat is reduced by 45% in a closing-down sale.
The sale price is £66.
Work out the price of the coat before the sale.

scheme.examinerNote: Follow through from the candidate's multiplier in part (a).

hints: Your multiplier from part (a) tells you what percentage the £66 is.

commonErrors.feedback: 45% of £66 was added on. The reduction of 45% was taken from £120, so it was £54, not £29.70. Divide by 0.55 instead.
Multiplying by 0.55 reduces the price a second time. To undo × 0.55, divide by 0.55.

context.setting: Two accounts at a credit union paying the same two rates

parts.stem:
A credit union pays 3% in the first year and 1.5% in the second year.
Niamh puts £2400 into an account.
Calculate the value of her account after two years.
hints: Year 2 acts on the balance at the end of year 1, not on the £2400.
£2472 × 1.015, then write the money to two decimal places.

commonErrors.feedback: The rates were added to 4.5%. Multipliers are applied one after the other: 1.03 × 1.015 = 1.04545.
The method is right; the money is not. £2509.08 needs both decimal places.

parts.stem:
Conor's account at the same credit union, with the same two rates, is worth £5227.25 after two years.
How much did Conor put into his account at the start?
hints: Part (a) ran the two multipliers forwards; this one runs them backwards.
Undo the second year first: £5227.25 ÷ 1.015 = £5150.
Then undo the first year: £5150 ÷ 1.03.

commonErrors.feedback: Both percentages were taken off the final balance. The interest was earned on smaller amounts, so each year has to be undone by dividing.
£5150 is the balance after one year, which earns the first mark. One more division by 1.03 reaches the opening deposit.

findTheMistake.stem: A tablet computer's price rose by 15%. The new price is £322. Erin was asked to work out the price before the rise. Her working:
findTheMistake.whatWentWrong: The 15% was worked out on the new price. The rise of 15% was added to the old price, which is smaller, so the rise was £42, not £48.30. Taking a percentage of the final value is the single most common zero-scoring start in this topic.
correction: The £322 comes after the rise, so 115% = £322
findTheMistake.feedback: Nothing is available here, because the first line decides the method and this one measures the percentage against the wrong amount. The line that earns the first mark is 115% = £322. Write the percentage the given value represents before you touch the calculator, then divide.

findTheMistake.stem: A jacket cost £96 last year and costs £120 now. Dara was asked to calculate the percentage increase. His working:
findTheMistake.whatWentWrong: The increase was divided by the new price. A percentage change is always measured against the amount the change started from, so the denominator is the £96, not the £120.
findTheMistake.feedback: One mark for showing the increase of £24, which is the line the November 2025 examiners said had to be present. The second mark is for dividing by the original. A quick test: multiply back. £96 × 1.20 = £115.20, not £120, so 20% cannot be right, while £96 × 1.25 = £120.

findTheMistake.stem: A large bag of dog food costs 18% more than a small bag. The difference between the two prices is £4.86. Maeve was asked to work out the cost of the large bag. Her working:
findTheMistake.whatWentWrong: Every line of the reversal is right: £27 is the small bag. The question asks for the large bag, which is the small bag plus the difference, £27 + £4.86 = £31.86.
findTheMistake.feedback: Three of the four marks: the set-up, the 1% and the 100% are all there, and the follow-through means the last mark is still available on a correct final step. Before you write anything on the answer line, read the question once more and name the quantity it asked for. Summer 2025 examiners reported this exact loss.

prompts.prompt: The three lines of a reverse percentage, in order.
prompts.answer: 1 Write the percentage the given value represents: (100 ± r)% = the value. 2 Divide by that percentage to reach 1%. 3 Multiply by 100. On a calculator the whole thing is one division by the multiplier.

prompts.prompt: Multiplier for an increase of $r\%$, and for a decrease of $r\%$?
prompts.answer: Increase: $1 + \frac{r}{100}$. Decrease: $1 - \frac{r}{100}$. An increase sits above 1, a decrease below it.

prompts.prompt: A price rose by 28% and you are told the new price. Is the new price 128% or 72% of the old one?
prompts.answer: 128%. An increase puts the value you are given above 100%; 72% would be a decrease of 28%.

prompts.prompt: What does depreciated mean, and what does it do to the percentage in the first line?
prompts.answer: Depreciated means fallen in value, so it is a decrease: the value you are given is below 100%. A fall of 6.2% makes it 93.8%.

prompts.prompt: An amount was multiplied by 1.35. What single operation returns the original amount?
prompts.answer: Divide by 1.35. Multiplying by 0.65 does not undo it: $1.35 \times 0.65 = 0.8775$.

prompts.prompt: You have reversed the percentage and found the original. What is the next thing to do?
prompts.answer: Read the question again and name the quantity it asks for. It may want the saving, the difference, the profit or the later price, and the original is only the middle of the working.
$\dfrac{\text{change}}{\text{original}} \times 100$. The change goes on top; the amount it started from goes underneath.

prompts.prompt: A bill is £72 including VAT at 20%. What is the bill before VAT?
prompts.answer: £72 ÷ 1.2 = £60. Including VAT means the 20% has already been added, so the £72 is 120%.

prompts.prompt: An account paid 5% in year one and 2% in year two, and now holds £5355. How do you find the opening deposit?
prompts.answer: Divide by each multiplier in turn: $5355 \div 1.02 = 5250$, then $5250 \div 1.05 = 5000$. Two changes need two divisions, and the rates are never added.

prompts.prompt: You have written 1% = £2.80 in a reverse percentage. What is still owed?
prompts.answer: × 100. The answer line wants 100%, so the original is £280; stopping at 1% loses the final mark.

prompts.prompt: A sale price of £68 after a reduction of 15% means £68 = ____% of the original price.
Your calculator shows 4820.5 for a money answer. What goes on the answer line?
prompts.answer: £4820.50. Money is written with two decimal places, and a missing trailing zero costs the accuracy mark.

findings.asked: Find the original value after an 18.2% decrease.
findings.wentWrong: Very few correct. Most found 18.2% of the given value and subtracted it. Those whose first line was 'given value = 81.8%' nearly always finished.
findings.fullMarkAnswersDid: Wrote the percentage the given value represents before calculating, then divided.
findings.rule: First line: the given value is (100 - 18.2)% of the original.

findings.asked: The same reverse-percentage question on M4.
findings.wentWrong: Mean mark two out of three; the same wrong start, taking the percentage of the final value, scored zero.
findings.rule: Never take a percentage of the final value in a reverse question.

findings.asked: The price before a 28% increase, given the new price.
findings.wentWrong: Recognition was poor in this series. Only the strongest equated the new price to 128% and divided to reach the three marks; some set the comparison up and then subtracted 28% anyway, which was the majority approach.
findings.fullMarkAnswersDid: Equated the new price to 128%, then divided by 1.28 (or found 1% and multiplied by 100).
findings.rule: Divide by 1.28; never subtract 28% of the new price.

findings.wentWrong: Well answered, but two zero-scoring starts recurred: 28% of the given value subtracted, or the given value equated to 72% instead of 128%. A few used the wrong number from the question.
findings.rule: An increase means the given value is more than 100% of the original.

findings.wentWrong: One of the poorest questions: few even equated the value to 90% for the first step; the usual approach was to add 10% on.
findings.rule: Reverse each change in turn, each time writing 'value = ...%'.

findings.wentWrong: About 37% full marks; most reversed only one of the two changes, or simply found 10% and subtracted then 15% and added.

findings.asked: A reverse percentage in an unusual wording, then a further step to the quantity asked.
findings.wentWrong: Pleasingly many found the original (24% = the difference, so 100% = 86), but then forgot to add the difference to reach the first-class fare, or subtracted it.
findings.rule: After the reverse step, re-read what quantity the question wants.

findings.wentWrong: Most correctly began with 112% = the given amount. The common slip afterwards was subtracting from the wrong value after increasing 900 by 17.6%; starting by finding 12% and subtracting scored nothing.
findings.rule: Keep track of which quantity each percentage refers to.

findings.asked: A percentage increase where the increase itself was given rather than having to be found (Foundation).
findings.wentWrong: A good discriminator that only the strongest answered. Adding the two values, or subtracting the smaller from the larger before dividing by the wrong figure, produced 108% and 92% far more often than the correct 8%.
findings.rule: Percentage change = change ÷ original × 100, and the original is the amount the change started from.

findings.asked: The same item on M2: the increase was stated in the question (Foundation).
findings.wentWrong: Many worked out an increase that had already been given. Dividing the larger number by the smaller to get 108% was widespread and earned nothing, because the answer needed was 8%.
findings.rule: New ÷ original is the multiplier as a percentage; the change is what is left above or below 100.

findings.wentWrong: Those who wrote 93.8% = given value usually finished; some set that up and then reverted to adding or subtracting 6.2%; others used 106.2% because 'depreciated' was not understood.
findings.rule: Depreciation is a decrease: the given value is below 100%.

findings.wentWrong: Most recognised it; those who did not either found 6.2% and subtracted or started from 106.2%.
findings.rule: Read the direction word before choosing the percentage.

findings.asked: Two banks paying a different rate in the first year and in each extra year.
findings.wentWrong: The second year was the problem: the rate was applied to the original deposit, or the two rates were added together and used once. Multiplier users struggled with 0.5%.
findings.rule: Each year's multiplier acts on the running balance; 0.5% is × 1.005 and rates are never added.

insight.ruleToRemember: Write '(100 ± r)% = the value you were given' as the first line, divide to reach 1%, multiply to reach 100% — or divide once by the multiplier. Decrease, discount, loss and depreciation all put the given value below 100%; increase, profit and VAT put it above. Two changes need two divisions, and rates are never added. Then read the question again and answer the quantity it asked for.
insight.aStarSignal: Two reversals in a row, or a reversal hidden in wording where the amount given is a difference rather than a total, followed by a correct final step to the quantity requested and money written to two decimal places.
